s: occurs_under the sun The speaker returns and sees all the oppressions done under the sun. They move him to judge the dead, and better still those never born who have not seen this evil work, as better off than the living.

is_a vanity [when driven by envy of a neighbor] Labor and achievement are said to be the envy of a man's neighbor, which makes them vanity. Better a handful with quietness than two handfuls with labor, and two people together have a good reward for their labor, while the solitary man's labor has no end and does not satisfy him.

The fool is a figure of folly described in Chapter 10: his heart sits at his left hand and his understanding fails as he walks, so he announces his own foolishness. His speech begins in foolishness and ends in mischievous madness; he multiplies words, is swallowed by his own lips, and is wearied by labor.

l: solitary man, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: A solitary man with no son or brother labors endlessly, his eyes never satisfied by wealth. He questions for whom he toils, denying himself enjoyment; this is called vanity and misery, and he has no one to help him when he falls.

l: two companions, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: A pair of companions is shown as better than a solitary person: they gain a good reward for their labor, lift each other when one falls, keep each other warm, and together withstand an attacker who would overcome one alone.
has_attribute not quickly broken [as a threefold cord] Companionship is shown to bring reward, help in falling, warmth, and defense. The text says a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

l: poor and wise youth, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: A poor, wise youth, declared better than an old, foolish king. Born poor in the kingdom, he rose from prison to rule. All the living walk with him and his successor, yet later generations will not rejoice in him.

l: old and foolish king, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: has_attribute unable to receive admonition The old and foolish king is judged worse than the poor and wise youth because he no longer knows how to receive admonition.
A vow to God is a binding obligation: it must be paid without delay, and not vowing is better than vowing and leaving it unpaid.

l: speech and words, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: A teaching on restraint in speech before God: words should be few, since many words bring vanity like many dreams, and the mouth must not cause sin, such as protesting a vow was a mistake.

l: riches and wealth, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: Riches are a topic of vanity: love of silver never satisfies, growing goods merely multiply consumers, hoarded wealth perishes through misfortune, and at death the owner carries nothing away, leaving as naked as he came.

l: rich owner of wealth, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: A rich man whose abundance denies him sleep, unlike the laborer. His only benefit is feasting his eyes; riches may perish, leaving his son nothing, and he departs naked, eating in darkness, frustrated and wrathful, unless God grants enjoyment.

is_enjoyed_as God’s gift [eating, drinking and enjoying good is one's portion] The sleep of a laboring man is sweet whether he eats little or much. Labor for the wind brings no profit at the end, but enjoying good in one's labor all the days God gives is called one's portion and something good and proper.

includes righteous and wicked receiving reversed outcomes Vanity is named in the burial and forgetting of the wicked, and in the case where the righteous and wicked receive each other's due. The narrator calls each of these also vanity.

l: man to whom God gives riches (Ecclesiastes 6:2), Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: A man given riches, wealth and honor, lacking nothing his soul desires, yet God gives him no power to enjoy them; a stranger eats them instead, called vanity and an evil disease.

l: man who fathers a hundred children, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: A man lives many years and fathers a hundred children, yet his soul is not filled with good and he lacks burial; the speaker deems a stillborn child better.

l: stillborn child, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: A stillborn child, described in Chapter 6, arrives in vanity and departs in darkness, its name covered. It never saw or knew the sun, yet is judged to have more rest than a man fathering a hundred children.

"Man" is portrayed as a frail, limited creature whose life is vain and passes like a shadow. He labors for his mouth yet is never satisfied, cannot contend with one mightier than himself, and cannot know what comes after him or his own time. Made upright, he seeks many inventions, is sinful, and has a heart full of evil. He is likened to fish and birds suddenly snared by an evil time. The account moves from toil and vanity, through sin and ignorance, to death: all go to one place, the dead, and his everlasting home, with dust returning to earth and spirit to God. It ends with his whole duty: fear God and keep his commandments, since every work and hidden thing will be judged.

l: the wise, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: The wise is a figure portrayed across Chapters 7, 8 and 10. His heart dwells in the house of mourning, and he welcomes rebuke over fools' song. Wisdom strengthens him beyond ten rulers, yet extortion can make him foolish. Wisdom makes his face shine, and his heart knows time and procedure, though he cannot find out the work under the sun. His heart is at his right hand, his words gracious, but a little folly can outweigh his honor.

l: the living, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: The living hold hope through their bond with all the living, though aware they will die; they are urged to enjoy bread, wine, garments, wife and labor.

l: house of mourning, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: is_better_than house of feasting [better to go to] It is said to be better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting, because it is the end of all men and the living should take it to heart. It is where the heart of the wise is found.

l: righteous man, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: The righteous man is a figure in Ecclesiastes who sometimes perishes despite his righteousness. The Preacher warns against excessive righteousness, noting no one on earth is sinless; later, some righteous men suffer the wicked's deserts, called vanity.

l: wicked man, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: has_fate lives long in evildoing [sometimes] A wicked man is observed to live long in his evildoing. The Preacher advises against being too wicked, asking why one should die before one's time.

l: the sinner, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: The wicked meet the same event as the righteous, and the sinner fares as the good do. The narrator notes that the hearts of men are full of evil and madness while they live, and that one sinner destroys much good.
A king whose word is supreme and who does whatever pleases him, unquestionable; the narrator counsels not hastily leaving his presence and keeping his command.

The wicked are a group who lack fear of God, so it will not go well with them and their days will not lengthen like a shadow. They are buried and forgotten despite long lives of crimes, and some receive the righteous's reward, which the narrator calls vanity.

l: those who fear God, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: has_fate better [better outcome than sinners] The narrator knows surely that it will be better with those who fear God and are reverent before him, even when sinners live long in their crimes.

l: king's command, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: is_to_be kept [because of the oath to God] The narrator says to keep the king's command because of the oath to God. Whoever keeps the commandment shall not come to harm.

l: work of God, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: The narrator saw that man cannot find out the work of God that is done under the sun. Even a wise man who claims he can comprehend it will not find it, however much he labors.

l: little city, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: has few men The little city had few men within it and was besieged by a great king who built great bulwarks against it. It was delivered by the wisdom of a poor wise man found in it.

l: the righteous, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: is_in_hand_of God The righteous, together with the wise and their works, are in the hand of God. They share the same event as the wicked, as the good do as the sinner, and the narrator counts this an evil under the sun.

l: the dead, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: The dead are described as knowing nothing, having no reward, and being forgotten; their love, hatred and envy have perished, leaving them no portion in anything done under the sun.

l: enjoyment of life, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: is_approved_by God [eating bread and drinking wine with joy] The narrator urges people to eat their bread with joy, drink wine with a merry heart, keep their garments white and their heads anointed with oil. He also urges them to live joyfully with the wife they love, since this is their portion in life and labor, and to do whatever their hand finds with all their might.

l: time and chance, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: happens_to man [all, regardless of strength, wisdom or skill] Time and chance happen to all, so that the race is not to the swift, the battle to the strong, bread to the wise, riches to the understanding, or favor to the skillful. Man does not know his time, and an evil time falls suddenly on people.

l: great king, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: besieges little city [built great bulwarks against it] A great king came against the little city, besieged it and built great bulwarks against it. The city was nevertheless delivered by the poor wise man.

l: poor wise man, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: A poor wise man in a little city delivers it by his wisdom, yet is afterward forgotten by everyone, and his wisdom is despised and his words go unheard.

is_source_of error [an evil seen under the sun] The ruler's spirit may rise up against a person, who is advised not to leave his place, since gentleness lays great offenses to rest. The speaker has seen an evil under the sun, a sort of error that proceeds from the ruler, in which folly is set in great dignity and the rich sit in a low place.

The king is a ruler whose character determines the land's fate: a child king, with princes feasting in the morning, brings woe, while a king born of nobles, with princes eating in due season for strength, brings happiness. The text ends by forbidding cursing him, even in thought, since a bird may report it.

l: young man, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: A young man is commanded to rejoice in his youth and follow his heart and eyes, yet is warned that God will judge all his deeds, so he should remove sorrow and evil.

is_advised_toward seven, even eight [giving a portion, given uncertainty of evil on earth] The unit urges casting bread on the waters, with the promise that it will be found after many days. It also advises giving a portion to seven, even to eight, because no one knows what evil will be on the earth.

l: uncertainty of the future, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: Uncertainty of the future is a topic: people cannot know what evil will come on the earth or which sowing will prosper, this, that, or both, just as they cannot know the wind's way, bones' growth, or God's work; dark days will be many.

l: sowing and reaping, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: A proverb-like teaching on sowing and reaping: those who watch wind and clouds hesitate and never sow or reap. The reader is urged to sow seed morning and evening, since it is unknown which will prosper or whether both succeed.
The unit states that God will bring the young man into judgment for all the things he does in following his heart and eyes. This is given as the counterweight to the call to rejoice in youth.

Youth is a topic in these records: a time to rejoice with a cheerful heart in Chapter 11, though called vanity, with sorrow and evil to be removed. Chapter 12 turns to the key charge: remember the Creator in youth, before the evil days come.

l: old age and death, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: Old age and death are portrayed in Chapter 12 as 'evil days' of fading pleasure: trembling, bowed bodies, few grinders, darkened windows, fear of heights, failing desire. Death follows when the silver cord is severed; mourners gather, dust returns to earth, and the spirit to God.

l: God's commandments, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: is_to_be kept [by man] God's commandments are to be kept, and doing so, together with fearing God, is called the end of the matter and the whole duty of man.

l: divine judgment, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher
s: covers every work [including every hidden thing, good or evil] God will bring every work into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether it is good or evil. This is given as the reason for fearing God and keeping his commandments.

The document is the Song of Solomon, eight chapters of love poetry attributed to Solomon, voiced mainly by a woman (the Beloved, once called the Shulammite) and her Lover, with interjections from Friends, the daughters of Jerusalem, and her Brothers. The Beloved and Lover matter most; Solomon appears as the named author and as a king in a wedding procession, and he is contrasted with her own vineyard at the end. Chapter 1 opens with the Beloved longing for her lover's kisses, calling his love better than wine, and describing herself as dark but lovely, made keeper of vineyards by her mother's sons. She asks where he pastures his flock; he answers and compares her to a steed in Pharaoh's chariots, and Friends promise gold earrings. Chapter 2 has her call herself a rose of Sharon, faint with love. She charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love before it desires, and recalls her beloved calling her away because winter is past. She declares he is hers and she his. Chapter 3 recounts her night search for him, her encounter with the watchmen, finding him and bringing him to her mother's house. A procession then comes up from the wilderness: Solomon's carriage, guarded by sixty mighty men, on his wedding day. Chapter 4 is the lover's praise of his beloved, called sister and bride, through images of doves, goats, pomegranate, and David's tower. He likens her to a locked garden, and she invites him into it. In Chapter 5 he enters his garden. She tells how she hesitated to open the door, found him gone, and was beaten by the watchmen. Asked by the daughters of Jerusalem what makes him special, she describes him as white and ruddy and altogether lovely. Chapter 6 has others offering to seek him with her; she says he has gone to his garden, and he praises her as unique among sixty queens, eighty concubines and countless virgins. Chapter 7 is an admiring description of her from feet to hair, comparing her stature to a palm tree. She replies that she is her beloved's and invites him to the fields and vineyards. Chapter 8 closes the book. She wishes he were her brother so she could kiss him openly, asks to be set as a seal on his heart, and declares that love is as strong as death and cannot be quenched by many waters. Her Brothers plan for their little sister, and she answers that she is a wall with breasts like towers. She ends by urging her lover to come away like a gazelle on the mountains of spices.

Beloved is a dark yet lovely young woman, the central female voice and subject of these records, who is in a mutual love with the Lover. She says the sun scorched her and that her mother's sons, angry with her, made her keeper of the vineyards while she did not keep her own. She calls the Lover the one her soul loves and likens him to a myrrh sachet between her breasts and a cluster of henna blossoms. The story opens with her longing to be kissed and taken into the king's rooms, and her asking where he grazes his flock. In the next stage the Lover describes her as an apple tree among the trees of the wood, calls her away to come, and asks to see her face and hear her sweet voice, comparing himself to a roe or young deer. He calls her a dove in the clefts of the rock. In the later stage she says he has gone down to his garden and declares that she is her beloved's and he is hers. He praises her as beautiful as Tirzah, lovely as Jerusalem and awesome as an army with banners. He calls her unique, her mother's only daughter and favorite, and says she is blessed by the daughters, queens and concubines. Finally she wishes she could kiss him openly as a brother, imagines leading him to her mother's house, and asks to be set as a seal on his heart and arm. She describes herself as a wall with breasts like towers, says her own vineyard is before her, and ends by urging him to come away like a gazelle or young stag on the mountains of spices.

The Lover is a central speaking figure in a poetic exchange of mutual devotion with the Beloved. The records present him as a king who brought her into his rooms, a keeper of a flock that he grazes and rests at noon, and someone born under an apple tree where his mother conceived him. He is called beautiful, likened to henna blossoms from the vineyards of En Gedi, and loved by virgins because of his name. His love is described as better than wine. The records also have him describe himself as a rose of Sharon and a lily of the valleys, and he is faint with love. The relationship is mutual belonging. In Chapter 1 he directs her to follow the sheep's tracks, compares her to a steed in Pharaoh's chariots, and praises her cheeks, neck, and doves' eyes. In Chapter 2 he calls the beloved to rise because winter is past, and charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up love before it desires. In Chapter 4 he calls her love, sister, and bride, says she has ravished his heart, and plans to go to the mountain of myrrh until the day is cool. In Chapter 6 he praises her as lovely as Jerusalem and awesome as an army with banners, and sets her above sixty queens and eighty concubines as his unique dove. In Chapter 8 he is the one she wishes to kiss and lean on, embracing her, dwelling in gardens with friends and asked to let her hear his voice. The records mix perspectives, with him both speaking and being described.

Solomon is a king, credited as the song's author and crowned by his mother on his wedding day. In Chapter 3 he owns a luxurious carriage of Lebanon wood, silver, gold and purple, and the daughters of Zion are told to see him crowned. In Chapter 8 he leases his Baal Hamon vineyard to keepers owing a thousand shekels each.

l: daughters of Jerusalem, The Song of Solomon
s: The daughters of Jerusalem are a chorus located in Jerusalem, addressed by the bride. In Chapter 3 they are adjured not to awaken love prematurely and are linked to Solomon's love-paved carriage. In Chapter 5 she adjures them to tell her beloved she is faint with love; they ask how he excels, prompting her description.

Love is described as better than wine, both by the Beloved speaking of her lover's love and by the Friends who say they will praise it more than wine. The virgins love the lover because his name is like oil poured out, and the Beloved says they are right to love him. The Beloved addresses him as the one whom her soul loves, and the Lover calls her "my love."

Love is portrayed as a overwhelming force. In Chapter 2 it is a banner over the speaker, who is faint with it, and it is expressed as mutual belonging: 'My beloved is mine, and I am his.' The daughters of Jerusalem are charged not to stir or awaken it before it desires. Chapter 8 climaxes: love is strong as death, fiery like a flame of the LORD, unquenchable by floods, and priceless beyond all wealth.

l: the beloved (him whom my soul loves), The Song of Solomon
s: He is sought by the speaker at night on her bed, but she does not find him. After she passes the watchmen she finds him, and she holds him and will not let him go until she brings him into her mother's house, into the room of her who conceived her.

l: the speaker (narrator, 'my soul'), The Song of Solomon
s: loves the beloved (him whom my soul loves) She seeks the one her soul loves at night, rises to search the city's streets and squares, and asks the watchmen if they have seen him. Having found him, she holds him and brings him to her mother's house. She then adjures the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up or awaken love until it so desires.

Love is the subject of the speaker's charge, that it not be stirred up or awakened until it so desires. It is also said to pave the middle of Solomon's carriage, coming from the daughters of Jerusalem.

l: carriage (Solomon's carriage), The Song of Solomon
s: Solomon's carriage, made by King Solomon of Lebanon wood with silver pillars, a gold bottom, and a purple seat, arrives from the wilderness like smoke pillars, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense. Its middle is paved with love, and sixty mighty men of Israel guard it.

l: mighty men of Israel (guards around Solomon's carriage), The Song of Solomon
s: Sixty mighty men of Israel, all expert in war and sword-skilled, surround Solomon's carriage, each carrying a sword on his thigh because of fear in the night.

l: Solomon's wedding day, The Song of Solomon
s: is_a day of gladness of Solomon's heart It is described as the day of Solomon's weddings and the day of the gladness of his heart. On it King Solomon wears the crown with which his mother has crowned him, and the daughters of Zion are called to go out and see him.

l: beloved (the bride's lover), The Song of Solomon
s: The beloved is the bride, also called sister as an endearment and likened to a locked-up garden. She is praised as beautiful and without spot, with detailed features: dove-like eyes, goat-flock hair, shorn-flock teeth, scarlet-thread lips, a tower-like neck, and fawn-like breasts. Her lips drip honey, milk lies under her tongue, and her garments smell of Lebanon. She is called away from Lebanon and said to have ravished the speaker's heart. At the end she invites the winds to blow on her garden and asks her beloved to come and taste its fruits.

l: garden (the Beloved's garden), The Song of Solomon
s: The bride is described as a locked up garden, a locked up spring, and a sealed fountain. Her shoots are called an orchard of pomegranates with precious fruits and spices such as henna, spikenard, saffron, calamus, cinnamon, myrrh, and aloes, and she is a fountain of gardens and a well of living waters. In the final verse she calls the north and south winds to blow on it so its spices flow out, and asks that her beloved come into his garden and taste its fruits.

is_addressed_by Friends [they call her to return] The Shulammite is called on by Friends to return, return so that they may gaze at her. The Lover responds by asking why they desire to gaze at her, as at the dance of Mahanaim.

l: prince's daughter, The Song of Solomon
s: The prince's daughter is praised in a detailed, head-to-toe address in Chapter 7. Her sandaled feet, thighs, body, waist, breasts, neck, eyes, nose, head and hair are each compared to something, such as jewels, a goblet, wheat, fawns, towers, pools and Carmel. Most notably, her hair holds the king captive in its tresses. Her stature is likened to a palm tree, and her mouth to the best wine. She is called beautiful and pleasant.

l: beloved (the speaker's beloved), The Song of Solomon
s: The beloved is the one to whom the woman declares she belongs, saying that his desire is toward her. She invites him to go out to the field, lodge in the villages and go early to the vineyards, where she will give him her love. She says that precious fruits, new and old, are at their doors, stored up for him.

l: Solomon's vineyard at Baal Hamon, The Song of Solomon
s: Solomon's vineyard at Baal Hamon, owned by him and leased to keepers, each of whom must bring a thousand shekels of silver for its fruit.

l: vineyard (the Beloved's own), The Song of Solomon
s: The Beloved's own vineyard is said to be before her, in contrast to Solomon's leased vineyard. She says the thousand are for Solomon and two hundred are for those who tend its fruit.

l: little sister (of the brothers), The Song of Solomon
s: A little sister, spoken of by her brothers, is immature and has no breasts. In Chapter 8 they ask what to do for her on the day she is spoken for, promising silver turret if wall, cedar boards if door.

This document is the book of Baruch together with the Letter of Jeremiah, a set of exilic writings addressed to Jews taken captive in Babylon. In Chapter 1, Baruch, son of Nerias, writes a book in Babylon in the fifth year after the Chaldeans burned Jerusalem and reads it to King Jechonias and the exiles by the river Sud. The people weep, fast, pray, and send money to Joakim the high priest and the priests in Jerusalem for offerings and for prayers for Nabuchodonosor and his son Baltasar. They ask that the book be read in the Lord's house as a confession that righteousness belongs to the Lord and shame to Judah, because the people, kings, priests, and prophets disobeyed him from the exodus onward. Chapter 2 continues the confession: the Lord has fulfilled his threats, including the horrors written in Moses' law. The people ask for mercy for his own sake, not their fathers' righteousness, and recall that refusing to serve Babylon brought desolation. They recall Moses' word that the stiff-necked people would be scattered but, repenting in captivity, would be restored to the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob under an everlasting covenant. Chapter 3 shifts from prayer to a meditation on wisdom. Israel forsook wisdom's fountain; rulers, wealthy men, giants, and foreign peoples never found her way, and only God, who knows all things, found her. He gave her to Jacob and Israel, and she appeared on earth and lived with men. Chapter 4 identifies wisdom with the book of God's commandments, the enduring law that gives life to those who keep it. Personified Jerusalem, a desolate widow, says her children were handed to a foreign nation for sacrificing to demons, then urges them to take courage and trust God's salvation. She promises doom for their oppressors and sees her sons returning. Chapter 5 turns to joyful consolation: Jerusalem is told to put off mourning and put on God's glory and righteousness, to be named 'Righteous Peace, Godly Glory,' and to see her children gathered from west to east, carried on a royal throne, with mountains made low and trees giving shade as God leads Israel in mercy and righteousness. The final piece, the Letter of Jeremiah, is sent to those about to be taken captive to Babylon. Jeremy says the captivity is punishment for sin, lasting seven generations, after which God will bring them out peacefully. He warns them not to fear or copy the silver, gold, and wooden idols they will see, mocking them at length as powerless and exploited by their priests, contrasts them with the sun, moon, stars, and elements that obey God, and concludes that the just man without idols is better.
Baruch, son of Nerias, wrote a book in Babylon in the fifth year after the Chaldeans burned Jerusalem, then read it aloud to Jechonias, the elders, mighty men, and people by the river Sud.

is_intended_for confession in the house of the Lord [read on feast days and solemn assemblies] The book is written in Babylon and read aloud to Jechonias and the exiles, who respond with weeping, fasting, and prayer. It is then sent to Jerusalem with money, to be read in the house of the Lord on feast days and days of solemn assembly as a confession of sin.

Babylon is the land of exile ruled by King Nabuchodonosor, who carried Jechonias, the princes, and the people there from Jerusalem. Baruch wrote and read his book there by the river Sud. The people confess they refused to serve its king as the prophets urged, so desolation came. The captives must remain for many years, seven generations, amid worshiped idols even the Chaldeans dishonor.

Jerusalem is a city personified as a mother of Israel's children. The records open with its capture and burning by the Chaldeans in Baruch's time, as exiles send money to Joakim the high priest and the book is read in the Lord's house. Jerusalem then speaks as a desolate widow in sackcloth, grieving her children's sins and trusting God to save them. She is told to take courage and look east for her sons' return. Finally she is commanded to remove mourning garments and put on the robe of righteousness and a diadem of glory. God will name her "Righteous Peace, Godly Glory" forever, as her children are gathered from west to east.
Jechonias, son of Joakim and king of Judah, was carried captive to Babylon by Nabuchodonosor with princes and mighty men, and is there when Baruch reads the book to him.

Nabuchodonosor is the king of Babylon and the Babylonians, father of Baltasar. He carried Jechonias and the people from Jerusalem into exile, and the exiles pray for his life and his son's, promising service.

God appears in these records as the righteous, everlasting Holy One and God of Israel, who made Israel, brought it up, and brought it out of Egypt with a mighty hand, signs and wonders. The account begins with the people's confession that righteousness belongs to the Lord while his wrath and indignation remain. He brought the fathers out of Egypt, declared a curse through Moses, and sent prophets whom the people did not heed. He is righteous in all his works, having fulfilled the word spoken through the law of Moses and the prophets by bringing plagues and scattering. The people appeal for mercy, recalling his promise through Moses of a heart and ears to hear, a return to the land promised to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and an everlasting covenant: he their God, they his people. He is provoked by their sacrifices to demons and delivers them to adversaries, though not to destroy them. Then the tone turns to comfort. As Everlasting Savior he promises to deliver Israel from enemies, punish the afflicting cities, and gather Jerusalem's sons. He calls Jerusalem by name, will show her splendor under heaven, and remembers her scattered children, carried back on high in glory. He levels mountains and hills and fills valleys so Israel may go safely, with trees shading them, and leads Israel with joy, mercy and righteousness. Finally, in the Letter of Jeremiah, his angel is with the captives, he cares for their souls, promises a peaceful return from Babylon, and commands the clouds, sun, moon, stars, wind and fire, unlike idols.
Exiles living by the river Sud serve Nabuchodonosor yet remain under the Lord's wrath for their sin; they hear the book, weep, fast, pray, send collected money to Jerusalem, and confess their sin.

Money collected by the exiles, each giving according to ability, and sent to Joakim the high priest and the priests in Jerusalem to buy burnt offerings, sin offerings, incense and oblation for the Lord's altar, when the temple vessels were returned to Judah.

Israel's sin and confession: the people acknowledge the Lord's righteousness and their own shame, admitting disobedience since the exodus from Egypt, ignoring the prophets, and serving strange gods by following wicked hearts, which brought plagues and the curse upon them.

Israel is portrayed as the people of God, called by his name, who are stiff-necked and have sinned, disobeying the Lord's voice, sacrificing to demons, and forsaking the fountain of wisdom. As a result they suffer plagues, reproach and a curse for the iniquities of earlier generations. God handed them to a foreign nation, Babylon, whose king they were commanded to serve, and they are scattered in an enemy land, few left among the heathen, with sons and daughters carried away. The account moves from confession in chapter 2, where they plead for deliverance because of God's name rather than their fathers' righteousness, to anguished prayer in chapter 3, where they are exhorted to hear the commandments of life and are told God gave them the way of knowledge. Chapter 4 says they were delivered to adversaries not for destruction but because they provoked God, and urges them to take hold of the law, endure patiently, seek God ten times more, and expect their enemy's fall. It ends in restoration in chapter 5: Israel walks safely in God's glory on level ground, shaded by sweet-smelling trees, led with joy, mercy and righteousness.

A punishment pronounced by the Lord against Israel's leaders and people, written in the law of Moses and unprecedented under heaven, including eating one's own children. The people acknowledge the plagues came as pronounced, killing kings and fathers by famine, sword, and pestilence. They then confess sin, admit their fathers disobeyed God, accept the penalty, and ask that their fathers' iniquities not be remembered.

The Lord scatters his people among surrounding nations, subjecting them to rival kingdoms as a reproach and desolation and reducing a great multitude to a few. In captivity they seek favor from captors, and as foretold through Moses, repent, know and praise the Lord, and return.

l: the land promised to the fathers, Baruch
s: is_given_to Israel [never again to be removed from it] The land was given to the people's fathers, and the prophets told the people to remain in it while serving the king of Babylon. Disobedience would make the cities of Judah and the region near Jerusalem desolate without inhabitant, silencing the voices of mirth, gladness, bridegroom, and bride. The Lord promises to bring them again into the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, where they will rule, increase, and never again be removed.

has_attribute stubbornness [Israel refuses to walk in the commandments] The people confess that they sinned against the Lord by not listening to his voice, not turning from the thoughts of their wicked hearts, and not walking in his commandments. They say they have been ungodly and done wrong in all his ordinances, and that they refused to serve the king of Babylon despite the prophets. Moses is recalled as describing them as stiff-necked, though they will eventually turn from their stiff neck and wicked deeds.

Wisdom is the fountain Israel forsook, a source of length of days and life. No one found her place: not princes, giants, the sons of Agar, or merchants, and none can fetch her from heaven or sea. Only God knows her; he gave her to Jacob and Israel, and she then appeared on earth, living with men.

Captivity is the condition of Israel's scattered children, brought upon them by God as penalty for their sins and their fathers' iniquities. It begins with the people reproached and cursed in enemy land, yet promising praise. It closes with Jerusalem mourning her children, carried off like a flock, and calling Zion's neighbors to remember.
The book of God's commandments is the law that endures forever: those who hold it fast live, those who leave it die. Israel's children were punished for turning from it and not walking in it.

A shameless, strange-tongued nation God brought from afar against Israel, merciless to old and young and carrying off the widow's children. The chapter foretells its destruction, with Israel treading on its necks, while the city that received Israel's sons is burned and desolate.

l: salvation and return of Israel, Baruch
s: God's promised salvation of the people: delivered from enemies' hands and returned to Jerusalem with everlasting joy. Those near Zion soon see salvation in great glory, and the sons are gathered from east to west, rejoicing in God's glory.

Jerusalem's children are seen gathered from the going down of the sun to its rising at the word of the Holy One, rejoicing that God has remembered them. They had gone from Jerusalem on foot, led away by their enemies, but God now brings them back carried on high with glory on a royal throne.

is_source_of_light_for Israel [God leads in its light] The glory of God is the beauty Jerusalem is told to put on forever, and the light in which God will lead Israel with joy. Israel is to go safely in it, and Jerusalem's name will include "Godly Glory". The children are brought back with glory, and a diadem of the glory of the Everlasting is set on Jerusalem's head.

Jeremy sends a letter to those about to be taken captive into Babylon, delivering God's commanded message: why they are taken, how long they will stay, and repeated warnings not to fear Babylonian idols.

Captives led to Babylon by Nabuchodonosor because of their sins will remain seven generations before God peacefully brings them out. Throughout, they are warned not to imitate foreigners or fear idols, and to say inwardly, 'O Lord, we must worship you.'

Babylonian idols are lifeless images of wood overlaid with silver and gold, fashioned by carpenters and goldsmiths and housed in temples. The Letter of Jeremiah shows them as powerless: they cannot speak, breathe, move unless carried, or save themselves from war, plague, or thieves. Inferior to sun, moon, and stars, they are declared no gods, so captives should not fear them.

The priests of Babylonian idols are portrayed as exploiting the idols they serve. They take gold and silver for themselves, give some to prostitutes, sell offered sacrifices, and clothe their own wives and children in the idols' garments. They lock temples against robbers, mourn with torn clothes and shaven heads, and plan to flee disasters, leaving the idols to burn.

is_characterized_as false [everything done among them is false] The letter argues that idol worship is futile because the idols are lifeless human creations that cannot act, judge, help, or defend themselves, and it repeatedly says "Therefore don't fear them." Those who serve them will be confounded, and the text concludes that the just man who has no idols is better, for he will be far from reproach.

The document is the Book of Joel, in three chapters, centered on the prophet Joel, son of Pethuel, and the LORD's word through him about the coming day of the LORD. Chapter 1 recounts an unprecedented locust devastation that strips vines, fig trees, grain and fields, silences joy, and cuts off offerings from the LORD's house. Joel summons elders, priests and ministers to wear sackcloth, fast, hold a solemn assembly and cry to the LORD, warning that destruction from the Almighty is at hand; he ends with his own cry as fire, drought and suffering animals mark the land. Chapter 2 opens with a trumpet alarm in Zion and the image of a vast, unstoppable army bringing darkness and fire. The LORD then calls his people to return with all their heart, tearing hearts rather than garments, because he is gracious and merciful. After a solemn assembly and the priests' plea, he becomes jealous for his land, removes the northern army, and promises grain, wine, oil, rain and restoration of the years the locusts ate. He also promises to pour out his Spirit on all flesh and save whoever calls on his name. Chapter 3 shifts to judgment: when Judah and Jerusalem are restored, the LORD gathers the nations into the valley of Jehoshaphat to judge them for scattering and selling his people. Tyre, Sidon and Philistia are singled out and promised repayment. The nations are summoned to war at the valley of decision, where the harvest of their wickedness is ripe and the heavens darken as the LORD roars from Zion, a refuge to his people. The book ends with Jerusalem holy, the land abundant, Egypt and Edom desolate for shedding innocent blood, and Judah inhabited forever because the LORD dwells in Zion.

The LORD is the gracious, merciful, slow-to-anger, loving God of Israel, who commands an invading army and dwells in Zion. In Joel 1, his word comes to Joel as offerings are cut off and destruction looms as the day of the LORD. In chapter 2, he thunders before his army, calls his people to return, then grows jealous for his land, pities them, promises grain, wine, oil, rain and restoration, and pledges to pour out his Spirit and save those who call on him. In chapter 3, he restores Judah and Jerusalem, judges the gathered nations, roars from Zion, and becomes Israel's refuge and stronghold, dwelling in Zion.

s: is_called_to cry to the LORD [gather at the house of the LORD] The elders and all inhabitants of the land are called to hear and to tell their children about an unprecedented calamity. They are later told to gather at the LORD's house for a solemn assembly and cry to the LORD. They suffer the loss of food, wine and joy.

l: locust plague, The Book of Joel
s: A locust plague in the Book of Joel, Chapter 1, described metaphorically as a strong, innumerable nation with lion's teeth. Successive waves of locust, grasshopper and caterpillar each eat what the previous left, laying waste the vine and fig tree, stripping bark and leaving branches white.
Priests are the LORD's ministers of the altar. In Joel 1, because meal and drink offerings are cut off from the LORD's house, they are commanded to wear sackcloth, wail, and lie all night mourning.

l: land of Joel's people, The Book of Joel
s: state laid waste [the land mourns] The land is laid waste and mourns as grain is destroyed, new wine dries up and oil languishes. A nation has come up on it, and fire has devoured the wilderness pastures. Its water brooks are dried up, and its livestock and flocks are desolate.

l: crops and trees, The Book of Joel
s: Crops and trees fail together: vine, fig, pomegranate, palm, apple and field trees wither, wheat and barley harvest perish, seeds rot, granaries and barns fall into ruin, and human joy withers with them.

l: day of the LORD, The Book of Joel
s: The day of the LORD is a prophesied event in the Book of Joel, announced as imminent destruction from the Almighty. It is great, very awesome, and a day of darkness and gloominess that no one can endure. Joel cries 'Alas for the day!', then describes the earth quaking, heavens trembling, and sun, moon, and stars darkened, the sun turning to darkness and the moon to blood. It culminates in judgment on the nations in the valley of Jehoshaphat, with repayment on Tyre, Sidon, Philistia, and desolation for Egypt and Edom.

l: fast and solemn assembly, The Book of Joel
s: A fast and solemn assembly, commanded in the Book of Joel, summons the elders and all the land's inhabitants to gather at the LORD's house and cry out. The LORD urges turning to him wholeheartedly, with fasting, weeping, and mourning, tearing hearts rather than garments, since he is gracious and merciful. It culminates with the priests weeping between porch and altar, begging him to spare his people.

Zion is the holy mountain, the LORD's dwelling, containing Jerusalem as a place of escape. It begins as the site where the alarm trumpet sounds and a solemn assembly is called, its children urged to rejoice, and ends with the LORD roaring from it and a fountain flowing out.
Jerusalem is a place whose children were sold to the Greeks, but its fortunes will be restored: it will become holy, free of strangers passing through, and inhabited across generations.

is_heritage_of LORD [his people and heritage] Israel is called the LORD's people and heritage, whom the nations scattered and whose land they divided. The LORD will be a stronghold to the children of Israel.

l: invading army (the LORD's army), The Book of Joel
s: The LORD's army is an unparalleled, great and strong northern people, horse-like and locust-like, marching in unbroken ranks. It advances with fire before and behind, scaling walls and entering houses like thieves, turning Eden-like land into wilderness. Finally, the LORD promises to drive it into a barren land and the eastern and western seas, where its stench rises.

l: people of Israel (the LORD's people), The Book of Joel
s: The children of Zion, the LORD's heritage, are summoned to tremble and assemble, from elders to nursing children, as priests plead against reproach among nations; the LORD pities them, promises satisfaction, and affirms they will know he is among Israel.

They are summoned to war and to the valley of Jehoshaphat, where the LORD will judge them for their great wickedness.

l: outpouring of the Spirit, The Book of Joel
s: The LORD promises that afterward he will pour out his Spirit on all flesh: sons and daughters prophesy, old men dream, young men see visions, and servants and handmaids also receive it.

l: restoration of harvest and rain, The Book of Joel
s: The LORD promises restoration after devastation: grain, new wine, and oil, with early and latter rain. Land and animals are told not to fear as pastures and crops revive. Threshing floors and vats fill, lost years from locusts are restored, and satisfied people praise the LORD.

will_be inhabited forever [future state] Judah's children were sold to the Greeks by Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia, but the LORD will stir them up from where they were sold and have them sell their enemies' sons and daughters to Sheba. Judah will be inhabited forever, its brooks will flow with water, and Egypt and Edom will be desolate for violence done to it.

l: valley of Jehoshaphat, The Book of Joel
s: The valley of Jehoshaphat, also called the valley of decision, is where the LORD will bring all nations down and sit in judgment, a crowded place where the day of the LORD is near.

l: restoration of Judah and Jerusalem, The Book of Joel
s: The restoration is the time the LORD announces when he will restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem, prompting the judgment of the nations. It is described as Jerusalem becoming holy, the land flowing with sweet wine, milk, and waters, and Judah and Jerusalem enduring forever.

This is the Book of Jonah, a four-chapter narrative about the prophet Jonah, son of Amittai, and his troubled obedience to the LORD. In chapter 1, the LORD commands Jonah to preach against Nineveh's wickedness, but he boards a ship at Joppa bound for Tarshish to flee. A great storm strikes; lots identify Jonah as the cause, and he tells the mariners to throw him into the sea. They do, the sea calms, they fear the LORD and offer sacrifice, and the LORD prepares a huge fish that swallows Jonah for three days and nights. In chapter 2, Jonah prays from inside the fish, recounting his affliction, remembering the LORD when his soul fainted, vowing thanksgiving, and declaring that salvation belongs to the LORD; the fish then vomits him onto dry land. In chapter 3, the LORD commands him a second time, and Jonah goes to Nineveh and proclaims its overthrow in forty days. The people believe God, fast and wear sackcloth, and the king sits in ashes and decrees that all, including animals, turn from evil and violence. God sees their works and relents. In chapter 4, Jonah is angry, explaining that he fled because he knew God is gracious and merciful, and asks to die. He waits east of the city; God provides a vine for shade, then a worm withers it, and Jonah again wishes to die. God contrasts Jonah's concern for a vine he did not labor for with His own concern for Nineveh's more than 120,000 people and many animals.

Jonah, son of Amittai, is a self-identified Hebrew who fears the LORD. Commissioned to preach against Nineveh, he flees toward Tarshish to avoid the mission. During a storm he is singled out by lot, tells the mariners to throw him into the sea, and is swallowed by a huge fish, staying three days and three nights in its belly. From there he prays, recalling his affliction, being brought up from the pit, and vowing sacrifice and thanksgiving, and he looks toward the holy temple. The fish vomits him onto dry land. Receiving the LORD's word a second time, he goes to Nineveh and proclaims its overthrow in forty days. He then becomes displeased and angry, explaining that he fled because he knew God is gracious, merciful, slow to anger and relenting of harm. He sits in a booth he made east of the city to watch, is glad for a vine, faints in the heat, and twice asks to die, insisting his anger is right.

The LORD is the God of heaven, maker of the sea and dry land, and the God of Jonah. He commands Jonah to go to Nineveh because of its wickedness. When Jonah flees, the LORD sends a storm, calms it when Jonah is thrown overboard, and prepares a fish that swallows him. Mariners fear and worship him. Jonah prays from Sheol, and the LORD has the fish vomit him onto land. Commanded a second time, Jonah preaches; the LORD sees Nineveh's repentance and relents. When Jonah grows angry, the LORD prepares a vine, a worm and an east wind to teach him, ending by affirming his concern for Nineveh, its people and animals.

Nineveh is a great city, three days' journey across, with over 120,000 people and many animals. Its wickedness comes up before the LORD, who tells Jonah to preach against it, though Jonah does not go at first. Later, warned of overthrow in forty days, the city repents and is spared when God relents. Jonah watches from the east, and God says He should be concerned for it.
Tarshish is the destination of the ship Jonah boards at Joppa, chosen as the place to flee from the LORD's presence. Jonah never arrives there in this unit.
Jonah pays the fare and boards the ship at Joppa, going down into it to travel to Tarshish. The storm makes it likely to break up, and the crew throw its cargo into the sea to lighten it.

The mariners are afraid in the storm, each crying to his own god, and they throw the cargo overboard. They cast lots, which fall on Jonah, question him, and row hard to reach land without success. They pray to the LORD not to be guilty of innocent blood, throw Jonah into the sea, and then fear the LORD, offer a sacrifice and make vows. Their ship master wakes Jonah and urges him to call on his God.

The LORD sends a great wind that causes a mighty storm on the sea, threatening to break up the ship. It grows more and more stormy while the men try to row to land, and Jonah says it is on them because of him. It ends when Jonah is thrown into the sea.

The sea is where the LORD sends the storm, and Jonah describes the LORD as the God who made it and the dry land. It grows more and more stormy until the mariners throw Jonah into it, whereupon it ceases its raging.
A huge fish prepared by the LORD that obeys him: it swallows Jonah, holds him three days and nights while he prays, then vomits him onto dry land at the LORD's command.

came_to holy temple [reached the LORD] Jonah's prayer, spoken from the fish's belly, recounts his cry in affliction, the LORD's answer, his sinking into the deep, and his rescue from the pit. It includes his remembering the LORD when his soul fainted, his claim that his prayer came to the LORD's holy temple, a remark that those who regard vain idols forsake their own mercy, and a vow to sacrifice with thanksgiving, ending with the declaration that salvation belongs to the LORD.

The inhabitants of Nineveh, over 120,000 people unable to discern right from left, believe God, fast, wear sackcloth, and turn from evil. God sees their works and spares them, citing them and their animals as reason for His concern.
The king of Nineveh, who rules the city, hears the news, abandons his throne and robe, wears sackcloth and sits in ashes, then with nobles decrees a fast and repentance, hoping God relents.
states Nineveh will be overthrown in forty days Jonah's message is a single cry: "In forty days, Nineveh will be overthrown!" It leads the people of Nineveh to believe God and repent.

is_practiced_by people of Nineveh [from greatest to least] The people proclaim a fast and put on sackcloth, and the king extends it by decree to man and animal, herd and flock, who are to taste nothing, drink no water, wear sackcloth, and cry mightily to God. It is joined with turning from evil ways and violence, and God sees these works and relents.

is_threatened_by The LORD [relented and did not carry it out] The disaster is the overthrow of Nineveh that God said he would do to them. Because the Ninevites turn from their evil way, God relents and does not carry it out.
A vine God prepares to shade Jonah's head, making him exceedingly glad; at dawn a God-prepared worm chews it and it withers, having come up in a night and perished in a night, unlabored for by Jonah.

has_intensity to death [Jonah claims he is right to be angry] Jonah's anger arises because the LORD relents of harm, and the LORD asks whether it is right. After the vine withers, Jonah says he is right to be angry even to death, and God contrasts his concern for the vine with His concern for Nineveh.

is_extended_to Nineveh [God asks whether he should be concerned] Jonah names God as gracious, merciful, slow to anger, abundant in loving kindness, and one who relents of doing harm. God shows this concern by arguing that He should be concerned for Nineveh's many people and animals, just as Jonah cared about the vine.

s: God is a architect (of created works)
q: They didn’t recognize the architect from his works.

s: God is more powerful than nature worship (fire, wind, air, stars, water, luminaries) (he formed the things worshipped)
q: then let them understand from them how much more powerful he who formed them is.

s: nature worship (fire, wind, air, stars, water, luminaries) is a belief that elements are gods ruling the world
q: But they thought that either fire, or wind, or swift air, or circling stars, or raging water, or luminaries of heaven were gods that rule the world.

s: Wisdom is a craftsman (who built the vessel)
q: wisdom was the craftsman who built it.

s: idols (works of men's hands) is subject to divine judgment (a visitation among the idols of the nation)
q: Therefore also there will be a visitation among the idols of the nation,

s: idols (works of men's hands) is temporary (did not exist from the beginning and will not exist forever)
q: For they didn’t exist from the beginning, and they won’t exist forever.

s: idols (works of men's hands) enters world through boastfulness of men (hence a speedy end was planned for them)
q: For by the boastfulness of men they entered into the world, and therefore a speedy end was planned for them.

s: idolatry is beginning of fornication (devising of idols)
q: For the devising of idols was the beginning of fornication, and the invention of them the corruption of life.

s: idolatry is beginning, cause and end of every evil (worship of idols that may not be named)
q: For the worship of idols that may not be named is a beginning and cause and end of every evil.

s: idolatry is hateful to God (along with the ungodly person)
q: For both the ungodly and his ungodliness are alike hateful to God;

s: idolatry originates from grieving father (image of his dead child honored as a god)
q: For a father worn with untimely grief, making an image of the child quickly taken away, now honored him as a god which was then a dead human being,

s: idolatry becomes law (custom grown strong, enforced by commandments of princes)
q: Afterward the ungodly custom, in process of time grown strong, was kept as a law, and the engraved images received worship by the commandments of princes.

s: worshipers is subject to divine judgment (for evil thoughts of God and unrighteous swearing)
q: But on both counts, the just doom will pursue them, because they had evil thoughts of God by giving heed to idols, and swore unrighteously in deceit through contempt for holiness.

s: worshipers practices madness, lying prophecy, unrighteousness and perjury (habitual conduct)
q: For their worshipers either make merry to madness, or prophesy lies, or live unrighteously, or lightly commit perjury.

s: God guides sailor (through providence, in the sea)
q: Your providence, O Father, guides it along, because even in the sea you gave a way, and in the waves a sure path,

s: worshipers trusts lifeless idols (expect no harm after wicked oaths)
q: For putting their trust in lifeless idols, when they have sworn a wicked oath, they expect not to suffer harm.

s: divine judgment is just (punishes the transgression of the unrighteous)
q: it is the just penalty for those who sin that always visits the transgression of the unrighteous.

s: divine judgment punishes idol maker (deed punished together with the doer)
q: for truly the deed will be punished together with him who committed it.

s: God has relationship to Wisdom (works of his wisdom are not to be ineffective)
q: It is your will that the works of your wisdom should not be ineffective.

s: God is able to save from every danger
q: showing that you can save out of every danger, that even a man without skill may put to sea.

s: wood is blessed (when it brings righteousness)
q: For blessed is wood through which comes righteousness;

s: wood is fragile (more fragile than the vessel that carries the sailor)
q: calls upon a piece of wood more fragile than the vessel that carries him.

s: idols (works of men's hands) is accursed (together with its maker)
q: but the idol made with hands is accursed, itself and he that made it;

s: idols (works of men's hands) is made from things God created
q: though formed of things which God created, they were made an abomination, stumbling blocks to the souls of men, and a snare to the feet of the foolish.

s: idols (works of men's hands) is abomination (stumbling block and snare to the foolish)
q: they were made an abomination, stumbling blocks to the souls of men, and a snare to the feet of the foolish.

s: God is gracious
q: But you, our God, are gracious and true, patient, and in mercy ordering all things.

s: potter judges use of each vessel
q: What shall be the use of each article of either sort, the potter is the judge.

s: potter molds idols (from the same clay as the vessels, to an evil end)
q: Also, laboring to an evil end, he molds a vain god out of the same clay,

s: potter is made of earth (returns to it and gives back the soul lent him)
q: he who, having but a little before been made of earth, after a short space goes his way to the earth out of which he was taken, when he is required to give back the soul which was lent him.

s: potter is ignorant of God (his maker)
q: because he was ignorant of him who molded him,

s: potter has heart of ashes
q: His heart is ashes.

s: potter regards life as a game (a festival for profit)
q: But he accounted our life to be a game, and our lifetime a festival for profit;

s: potter knows he sins (beyond all others)
q: For this man, beyond all others, knows that he sins, out of earthy matter making brittle vessels and engraved images.

s: idols lack senses and mobility (no eyes, nostrils, ears, fingers, or walking feet)
q: which have neither the use of eyes for seeing, nor nostrils for drawing breath, nor ears to hear, nor fingers for handling, and their feet are helpless for walking.

s: idols is made by man (mortal with borrowed spirit)
q: For a man made them, and one whose own spirit is borrowed molded them;

s: idols is a dead thing (never had life)
q: But, being mortal, he makes a dead thing by the work of lawless hands; for he is better than the objects of his worship, since he indeed had life, but they never did.

s: God is true
q: But you, our God, are gracious and true, patient, and in mercy ordering all things.

s: idols is considered god by enemies of God's people (also by the nations)
q: because they even considered all the idols of the nations to be gods,

s: enemies of God's people oppressed God's people (Israel, your sons)
q: But most foolish and more miserable than a baby, are the enemies of your people, who oppressed them;

s: enemies of God's people is most foolish (more miserable than a baby)
q: But most foolish and more miserable than a baby, are the enemies of your people, who oppressed them;

s: idol worship leads fools (into lust, via painted image)
q: the sight of which leads fools into lust.
